title: Order of Operations for Grade 5: BODMAS Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_title: Order of Operations Grade 5 BODMAS Explained + Quiz
meta_desc: Order of operations for Grade 5 made simple with BODMAS: what it means, why order matters and common mistakes, plus a free 8-question quiz to try.
excerpt: Two children, one expression, two different answers. That is the moment BODMAS earns its place. Here is order of operations for Grade 5 explained plainly, with a worked-example table and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Two Grade 5 students, same question on the board: 6 + 2 × 3. One writes 24, the other writes 12. Both are certain they are right. This is exactly where order of operations for Grade 5 and the BODMAS rule earn their keep — without an agreed order, one expression gives two answers, and only one is correct. (It is 12, and the reason is coming.)

By Grade 5 children start meeting expressions with two, three, sometimes four operations jumbled together. This is where mixed calculations get introduced properly, and it is the foundation for everything from fractions to algebra later on. Get the order wrong now and the mistakes quietly compound for years. The good news: BODMAS is a short, fixed set of rules, and once a child understands why the order exists, they stop guessing.

What BODMAS actually stands for

BODMAS is a memory aid for the order in which we work through a calculation. Some schools teach BIDMAS instead — same rule, the I stands for Indices, which is just another word for Orders. Here is each letter.

LetterMeaningExample
BBrackets ( )(4 + 2)
OOrders / of — powers and ‘of’3², half of 8
DMDivision and Multiplication, left to right12 ÷ 3, 4 × 5
ASAddition and Subtraction, left to right7 + 5, 9 − 2

The single most misunderstood part is the DM and AS pairs. Division does not always come before multiplication, and addition does not always come before subtraction. Within each pair the operations rank equally, so you simply work left to right. More on that trap below.

Why the order matters

Back to 6 + 2 × 3. Go strictly left to right — the instinct of almost every beginner — and you get 6 + 2 = 8, then 8 × 3 = 24. But BODMAS settles multiplication before addition, so 2 × 3 = 6 first, then 6 + 6 = 12. Same digits, same symbols, two very different answers. The order is not a fussy rule invented to trip children up; it is the shared agreement that lets everyone read the same expression the same way.

A quick way to prove it to your child

Ask them to buy 2 packets of biscuits at ₹3 each and add a ₹6 chocolate. The cost is 6 + 2 × 3 = ₹12, not ₹24. Money makes the ‘multiply first’ rule feel obvious rather than arbitrary. I lean on shopping examples constantly for this — they turn an abstract rule into something a ten-year-old can picture.

Brackets come first, always

Brackets are the override switch. Anything inside them is calculated before anything outside. Compare these two:

  • 6 + 2 × 3 = 6 + 6 = 12 (multiply first, no brackets)
  • (6 + 2) × 3 = 8 × 3 = 24 (brackets force the addition first)

So the ‘wrong’ answer of 24 is actually correct — but only when brackets are there to demand it. Teaching these side by side works well, because the child sees that brackets are how we change the order on purpose.

The left-to-right trap

Here is the mistake I see most in Grade 5 books. A child faces 20 ÷ 4 × 5 and reasons ‘D comes before M in BODMAS, so divide then multiply’ — which by luck gives the right answer here. But hand them 20 − 8 + 3 and the same faulty logic says ‘A before S’, so 8 + 3 = 11 first, then 20 − 11 = 9. Wrong. Worked left to right it is 20 − 8 = 12, then 12 + 3 = 15.

Drill one sentence until it sticks: multiplication and division are a team worked left to right, and so are addition and subtraction.

Worked examples to model out loud

ExpressionFirst stepThenAnswer
8 + 4 × 24 × 2 = 88 + 816
(8 + 4) × 28 + 4 = 1212 × 224
20 − 8 + 320 − 8 = 1212 + 315
36 ÷ (2 + 4)2 + 4 = 636 ÷ 66
5 × 3 − 45 × 3 = 1515 − 411

Common mistakes to watch for

  • Working strictly left to right and ignoring BODMAS entirely.
  • Believing division must always beat multiplication, or addition must always beat subtraction.
  • Forgetting to finish everything inside the brackets before moving on.
  • Rushing a multi-step sum instead of writing one clean line per step.
  • Reading ‘of’ (as in half of 8) as a low-priority word rather than treating it like multiplication near the top of the order.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The eight questions below use only whole numbers and the four operations with brackets — no negatives, exactly Grade 5 level. Let your child solve each one on paper, one step per line, then read the explanation for anything they miss. When they are ready for more, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded BODMAS practice with a full answer key.

quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on BODMAS with brackets, multiplication, division, addition and subtraction. Work each one on paper, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 5 order of operations with BODMAS

questions.explanation: Addition and subtraction rank equally, so work left to right: 20 − 8 = 12, then 12 + 3 = 15.
Division and multiplication rank equally, so left to right: 20 ÷ 4 = 5, then 5 × 5 = 25.

questions.q: In 7 + 10 ÷ 5, which part do you calculate first?
questions.explanation: Division comes before addition, so 10 ÷ 5 = 2 is done first, then 7 + 2 = 9.

faq.a: Brackets, Orders (powers and ‘of’), Division and Multiplication, then Addition and Subtraction. Division and multiplication rank equally and are done left to right, and so are addition and subtraction.

faq.q: Is BODMAS the same as BIDMAS or PEMDAS?
faq.a: Yes, they are the same rule with different names. BIDMAS uses I for Indices instead of O for Orders, and PEMDAS (common in the US) uses P for Parentheses and E for Exponents. The working order is identical.

faq.q: Does division always come before multiplication?
faq.a: No — this is the most common Grade 5 error. Division and multiplication have equal priority, so you work them left to right. The same is true for addition and subtraction.

faq.q: Why do we even need order of operations?
faq.a: Without a shared order, one expression could give many answers. Take 6 + 2 × 3: BODMAS fixes it at 12 so that every student, teacher and calculator reads it the same way.
